extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and using transitions (words, phrases, sentences, or paragraphs) to establish logical connections between sentences, paragraphs, and sections in academic or professional writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and importance of transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions glue ideas and essays together by establishing logical connections between sentences, paragraphs, and sections; they tell readers what to do with the information you present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitions to convey relationships (e.g., 'Another example coming up—stay alert!' or 'Here’s an exception to my previous statement') and to provide cues that help readers understand how ideas fit together. Transitions are not mere decorations; they have particular meanings that direct reader reaction and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions must reflect and reinforce organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions cannot substitute for good organization; their clarity and effectiveness depend on how well the paper is organized (order of parts and relationships between parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before working on transitions, evaluate organization by summarizing each paragraph in the margins (reverse outlining). If paragraphs don't logically connect, fix organization first; transitions highlight relationships that already exist rather than create coherence from disorganized material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs you need to work on transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clues that transitions are weak include instructor comments like “choppy,” “jumpy,” “abrupt,” or readers saying they had trouble following the organization or train of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other signs: writing that mirrors rapid internal thought jumps, assembling a paper by pasting discrete chunks, or working on group papers that combine multiple writers' drafts. Use these as prompts to check transitions and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: How transitions work (summarize then anticipate)
rubrics_metrics.description: A transition either directly summarizes preceding content or implies such a summary, then helps the reader anticipate or comprehend the new information to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitions to indicate the specific logical connection (e.g., contradiction, continuation) between two paragraphs or sections. Example: to link a paragraph that lists reasons El Pais seems democratic to one that refutes those reasons, use a transition like 'Despite the previous arguments,' to signal contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of transitions by scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions can be a single word, a phrase, a sentence, or an entire paragraph; they function similarly across scales by summarizing what came before and orienting the reader to what comes next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the scope of transition based on distance and complexity of the shift: use paragraph-long transitions for major sectional shifts and single words/phrases for small intra-paragraph shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions between sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer works may require transitional paragraphs that summarize the information just covered and specify its relevance to the following section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitional paragraphs to prepare readers for a major change in topic or new stage of argument, explicitly connecting prior material to the upcoming section's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions between paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: If paragraphs are arranged so one leads logically to the next, the transition highlights the existing relationship by summarizing the previous paragraph and suggesting content of the following one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transition between paragraphs can be a word or two, a phrase, or a sentence; it may appear at the end of the first paragraph, at the beginning of the second, or both. Examples: 'however,' 'for example,' 'similarly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions within paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Within paragraphs, transitions act as cues to help readers anticipate what is coming before they read it; they tend to be single words or short phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short linking words and phrases to move between ideas within a paragraph so the reader can follow the internal logic and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transitions that signal similarity to link comparable ideas or examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'also,' 'in the same way,' 'just as … so too,' 'likewise,' 'similarly.' Choose the precise phrase that matches the degree/type of similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception/Contrast transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transitions that mark contrast or exceptions when the following idea contradicts or qualifies the previous one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'but,' 'however,' 'in spite of,' 'on the one hand … on the other hand,' 'nevertheless,' 'nonetheless,' 'notwithstanding,' 'in contrast,' 'on the contrary,' 'still,' 'yet.' Use these to signal opposing or qualifying relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence/Order transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words that indicate sequence or order to structure steps, reasons, or items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'first,' 'second,' 'third,' 'next,' 'then,' 'finally.' Useful for enumerating points or showing procedural/order relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use temporal transitions to place events or claims in time relative to one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use example signals to introduce an instance or illustration of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'for example,' 'for instance,' 'namely,' 'specifically,' 'to illustrate.' These cue the reader that concrete evidence or illustration follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use emphasis transitions to highlight an important point or to strengthen a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'even,' 'indeed,' 'in fact,' 'of course,' 'truly.' Use sparingly to avoid overstating or redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place/Position transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transitions that indicate spatial relationships or positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'above,' 'adjacent,' 'below,' 'beyond,' 'here,' 'in front,' 'in back,' 'nearby,' 'there.' Useful in descriptive or spatially organized writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and effect transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transitions that signal causal relationships between ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'accordingly,' 'consequently,' 'hence,' 'so,' 'therefore,' 'thus.' Employ to make logical consequence clear and to link claims with outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional support or evidence transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transitions that add support or further evidence for a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'additionally,' 'again,' 'also,' 'and,' 'as well,' 'besides,' 'equally important,' 'further,' 'furthermore,' 'in addition,' 'moreover,' 'then.' Use to build cumulative support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion/Summary transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transitions that indicate summary or closure to wrap up points or sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'finally,' 'in a word,' 'in brief,' 'briefly,' 'in conclusion,' 'in the end,' 'in the final analysis,' 'on the whole,' 'thus,' 'to conclude,' 'to summarize,' 'in sum,' 'to sum up,' 'in summary.' Use to signal synthesis or end of discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose precise words and verify meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Different transitional words or phrases may have slightly different meanings; be sure to select the one that matches the relationship you intend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure of exact meaning, consult a dictionary or writer's handbook (or the handout for multilingual writers) to ensure the transition conveys the intended logical relationship.
